that different types of feedback are better suited for different phases of inquiry activities. While

the orientation phase generally requires little guidance, many different types of scaffolds and

supports have been designed for the conceptualization and investigation phases but little

empirical evidence exists in support of their efficacy in applied settings (Zacharia et al., 2015).

Guidance must be delivered in appropriate forms and according to the needs of the student

(Belland & Drake, 2013), but extant literature is sparse regarding what these optimal forms and

customizations are for science education. A meta-analysis of this literature for feedback systems

in all types of computer-supported learning environment indicated that elaborated feedback is

generally more effective than feedback specifically on correctness or when systems provide a

“correct” answer (Van der Kleij et al., 2015), and that immediate feedback is generally more

effective than delayed feedback.

16

Worked examples are another form of hint popular in ITS and games. While worked

example-based feedback is generally as effective as tutored problems and showing erroneous

examples, worked examples are by far the most efficient form of feedback (McLaren et al.,

2015). While this finding was from stoichiometry problem solving in a chemistry tool and not an

inquiry-based environment, the efficiency of feedback and hint tools is an important

consideration during time-constrained interventions or curricula. Worked examples are typically

effective in aiding deep understanding when presented during initial skill acquisition, although

worked examples are best used when combined with prompts and suggestions to encourage self
explanation of the examples (Renkl, 2014).

It is essential that students using conceptually-integrated games or environments (where

learning content is fully embedded in manipulating the virtual space) are able to relate their in
game actions to formal learning goals (Clark & Martinez-Garza, 2012; Habgood & Ainsworth,

2011), and one way to make that relationship explicit is through self-explanation of their

problem solving processes. Self- explanation encourages students to engage in deeper learning

by exploring what they do and do not know, and it has been shown especially effective in

multimedia environments (Roy & Chi, 2005). These tasks run the risk of increasing cognitive

load of learners, but steps such as offering learners self-explanation options or scaling the

abstraction of prompts based on past learner performance can mitigate this issue (Adams &

Clark, 2014; Clark et al., 2016). Both very simple and very abstract self-explanation prompts are

not useful, indicating an optimal level of reflection and introspection that is useful during game
based learning (O’Neil et al., 2014). Self-explaining (along with note taking and concept

mapping) has been shown to increase student engagement learning material in an attempt to

increase learning (Chi & Wylie, 2014).

17

While the ability to generate feedback automatically is exciting, ensuring the helpfulness

of that feedback for the learner is paramount. For example, providing hints where none are

needed or providing high-level guidance where a learner is struggling with something

foundational are both unhelpful. While prohibitively difficult in the past, fitting models in real
time on individual students based on their early actions is becoming more feasible (Koedinger et

al., 2013). This could allow initial hints to be more on-target; initial hint quality is very important

to reducing negative behaviors in open-ended problems (Price et al., 2017). Early hints are

typically seen by more students, help on post-test performance when compared to control groups,

and have also been shown to promote near-transfer between problems and improve later

performance (Stamper, Eagle, Barnes, & Croy, 2013). In general, bad hints (e.g., ones that

incorrectly diagnose issues or increase cognitive load) are worse than no hints at all, and the

earlier an appropriate hint is delivered, the larger impact it has on learning.

In addition to content-area experts rating hint quality, feedback and involvement of the

teacher in formal educational settings is becoming increasingly more common in hint generation.

By showing teachers a list of issues and suggested help automatically detected from a class, they

can then change what types of hints are being shown or how often these appear, based on

understanding of the prior knowledge of classes or their perceptions of student competence (Ben
Naim et al., 2009). Feedback can be directed toward specific misconceptions seen in multiple

cases in the class, so the expertise of the teacher can be leveraged in a tutor environment.

results.summary:
Published May 17, 2026 | Version v1

Journal Open

# Personalizing STEM Learning at Scale: An Adaptive AI Tutoring Suite with Student Modeling, Curriculum Sequencing, and Explainable Formative Feedback

## Description

Personalized, real-time instruction in STEM classrooms remains a persistent challenge: student cohorts vary widely in prior knowledge and misconception patterns, while teachers lack timely, individualized data to adapt instruction dynamically. This paper presents the Adaptive Tutoring Suite (ATS), a modular AI-driven platform designed to improve measurable learning outcomes in STEM micro-learning environments. The ATS integrates four evidence-informed components: (1) a hybrid Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) and transformer-embedding student model that produces calibrated, real-time mastery estimates; (2) a constrained curriculum sequencing engine combining Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming (MIQP) with an online contextual bandit to minimize expected lessons-to-mastery under classroom resource constraints; (3) an explainable automated formative feedback pipeline that fuses large language model (LLM) outputs with symbolic validators to generate accurate, actionable hints; and (4) a teacher-facing dashboard providing intervention recommendations and a feedback review queue. We evaluate the ATS using publicly available datasets (ASSISTments, EdNet) and parameterized synthetic classroom cohorts, reporting mastery prediction accuracy, normalized learning gain, time-to-mastery reduction, and feedback utility. Results from simulation and ablation analyses indicate that the hybrid student model improves mastery calibration over standard BKT, the MIQP-bandit sequencer reduces expected instructional time compared to greedy baselines, and the hybrid feedback pipeline achieves higher teacher-rated hint utility with fewer high-confidence errors than an LLM-only approach. Implications for scalable, equitable personalization in STEM education and directions for real-world classroom deployment are discussed.

results.title: Diagnosing Student Misconceptions for Targeted Feedback — Lacuna

# Diagnosing Student Misconceptions for Targeted Feedback

When a student fails to solve an educational task, traditional software records a binary zero. But a wrong answer is rarely random noise; it is usually the logical output of a flawed internal mental model. For example, if a student calculates $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{5}$, they have not simply failed—they have systematically applied a "mal-rule" (adding numerators and denominators directly).

Misconception modeling shifts the paradigm from tracking whether a student succeeded to diagnosing why they failed. By treating errors as structured evidence of a learner's internal state, intelligent tutoring systems and educators can deliver surgical, context-aware remediation instead of generic repetition.

## Extracting Signal from Mistakes

Standard knowledge tracing frameworks often treat all incorrect choices identically, discarding rich evidence regarding the underlying cognitive process leading to an error. However, multiple-choice distractors and free-text responses frequently encode highly predictable misconceptions.

As Aritra Ghosh et al. demonstrate in Option Tracing: Beyond Correctness Analysis in Knowledge Tracing, modeling specific incorrect choices in multiple-choice assessments reveals structured patterns of student reasoning that are completely lost in binary correctness analysis. By analyzing the exact option a student selects, systems can isolate systematic errors in reasoning rather than just recording a failure to answer correctly.

To maximize this diagnostic signal, S. Park et al. introduce a response disentanglement mechanism in Enhancing knowledge tracing with concept map and response disentanglement. This approach isolates specific student misconceptions by encoding the selected multiple-choice option and subtracting a representation of the unchosen alternatives. This disentanglement allows the model to capture the qualitative reasoning behind an error.

Shifting from aggregate scoring to granular item-level tracking allows for surgical pedagogical interventions. As Ling Chen highlights in Using Online Tests to Enhance Teaching and Learning, tracking specific student responses and error patterns across individual items allows instructors to identify precise conceptual bottlenecks within a cohort—such as difficulty distinguishing between specific technical categories—and pivot their teaching strategies in real-time.

## Tracing the Problem-Solving Process

While final answers provide clues, the true nature of a misconception often reveals itself sequentially. Process-oriented diagnosis analyzes the specific steps a student takes during problem-solving to distinguish between simple execution slips (like arithmetic typos) and fundamental conceptual errors.

In Using Inverse Planning for Personalized Feedback, Anna N. Rafferty models the sequential steps a learner takes to solve a problem using a Bayesian inverse planning framework. By explicitly incorporating common procedural misconceptions, or mal-rules, into the model's hypothesis space, the system can diagnose the exact nature of a learner's struggle rather than simply marking a step as incorrect.

This works by comparing the student's step-by-step reasoning against an internal expert solver's logic. As Liu Zhang et al. show in Computer Simulation of Statistics and Educational Measurement StatSim: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Statistics, identifying the precise point where a learner's logic diverges from expert reasoning allows the system to pinpoint the root cause of the struggle. Instead of marking an entire multi-step problem as wrong, the system uncovers the exact transition where the flawed mental model took over, providing a pathway for targeted feedback.

## The Pedagogical Payoff

The ultimate value of misconception modeling lies in its ability to inform instruction, whether delivered by a human teacher or an automated agent. Performance metrics that only track completion or general success fail to explain the specific reasons behind student failure, leaving educators without the diagnostic information needed to plan effective interventions.

In Developing a Teacher Dashboard For Use with Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Vincent Aleven et al. find that teachers prioritize identifying specific student misconceptions over simple progress tracking. Understanding the underlying cause of errors enables educators to pivot from individual monitoring to executing focused whole-class mini-lessons or targeting specific sub-groups.

Similarly, Ken Holstein et al. demonstrate in Luna: A Dashboard for Teachers Using Intelligent Tutoring Systems that visualizing specific logic errors provides more actionable pedagogical value for teachers than aggregate mastery scores.

In automated environments, this precision prevents the delivery of irrelevant or confusing feedback. As Alexander Scarlatos et al. note in Improving the Validity of Automatically Generated Feedback via Reinforcement Learning, models must distinguish between different types of misconceptions for the exact same problem to provide relevant guidance rather than generic mathematical advice.

With the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into educational technology, a new challenge has emerged: models are highly capable of generating correct answers, but they struggle to reason about incorrect logic.

results.summary:
More recent advances such as DenoiseKT [7] and MASKT [24] focus on robustness, with the former reducing noise via denoised attention and question- augmented representations, and the latter leveraging multi- layer attention with self- supervised noise tolerance to capture richer student- concept interactions [1]. These advances enabled models to capture rapid shifts and irregular fluctuations in students' knowledge states, which earlier approaches could not handle effectively. However, both approaches still rely on a single reasoning path and cannot explicitly represent prerequisite- dependency structures, leading to errors in complex concept chains or sparse interactions, and their outputs rarely translate into personalized interventions.  

### 2.2 Graph-based and Causal Extensions  

Building on sequential models, later work introduced graph- based and causal approaches to address the lack of structural bias. GRKT [6] leverages graph neural networks to encode prerequisite relations between knowledge concepts, while DyGKT [3] dynamically updates these graphs to capture changing student- concept interactions. CPF [26] introduces a personalized forgetting mechanism driven by causal assumptions to better model knowledge decay.  

Compared with the sequential methods in the previous section, these approaches shift from purely temporal reasoning to structurally informed reasoning [34]. This allows educational systems to better capture prerequisite relations among concepts and reduce misdiagnosis in long concept chains or sparse interaction scenarios. However, these approaches remain limited in scope, as graph reasoning is often used in isolation and updates are largely heuristic or static. As a result, the predictions and interventions remain loosely connected, and the models cannot yet form a genuine closed- loop learning system.  

### 2.3 Closed-loop and Personalized Feedback  

While graph- based methods improved structural reasoning, they still focused mainly on diagnosis [9][31]. More recent studies have taken a further step by attempting to link this diagnosis with feedback generation, aiming to close the gap between predicting student states and providing adaptive guidance. For example, GPT- based Auto- Grader employs large language models to score short- answer questions by comparing student responses with reference answers and grading rubrics, reducing manual grading effort. In contrast, NaviEdu integrates dual-path causal inference and closed-loop feedback: it can detect abrupt changes in performance, identify the underlying prerequisite gap, and immediately transform this diagnosis into targeted, step-by-step interventions.

Aligned LLMs[21], in contrast, focus on generating feedback that follows established teaching principles, aiming to ensure that the advice provided to students is not only linguistically correct but also educationally meaningful[17]. Compared with the previous graph- only methods, these approaches go beyond pure diagnosis by directly linking predictions with instructional actions. They enable systems to not only estimate a student's knowledge state but also deliver concrete guidance, such as automated grading of short answers or feedback that highlights misconceptions and suggests targeted practice.  

However, their feedback and knowledge tracing remain loosely coupled. In practice, this often leads to delayed or generic advice, as the feedback module is added after prediction rather than integrated into the inference process. A critical error case illustrates this: when the same student shows a sudden change in performance on the same concept (e.g., consistently correct before but then several mistakes in a row), current systems either overfit the noise if relying mainly on neural signals, or react too slowly if relying mainly  

on structural graphs, which results in a misdiagnosis by treating true knowledge decay as random fluctuation. To reduce such misdiagnoses, NaviEdu combines neural and graph causal paths with consistency alignment and gradient- sensitivity, enabling real- time graph updates and personalized interventions.  

## 3 Methodology  

### 3.1 Framework Overview  

Existing knowledge tracing models often struggle with two persistent issues: they either rely on a single reasoning paradigm, which makes it difficult to jointly capture non- linear learning dynamics and structured concept dependencies, or they treat diagnosis and intervention as separate steps, leaving the feedback loop incomplete. These limitations lead to frequent misdiagnosis in practice, for example, confusing genuine knowledge decay with random fluctuations. To address this, in NaviEdu as shown in Fig. 2, the consistency errors and gradient- sensitivity signals from dual- path

reasoning are simultaneously used to update the dynamic knowledge graph, linking feedback with inference in parallel and thus shortening the gap between diagnosis and intervention.

### 2.2 Self-regulated learning as the process model  

Self- regulated learning (SRL) describes how learners set goals, plan, monitor performance, use strategies, and reflect on results. Models differ in terminology, but generally treat learning as a cycle rather than a single act of content consumption (Panadero, 2017). Analytics can support this cycle by helping learners notice a gap, select a strategy, monitor its effect, and revise a plan. They can also undermine it if learners become passive recipients of automated prescriptions or learn to optimise the visible metric rather than the underlying capability.  

Evidence about analytics interventions reflects this imbalance. In a systematic review of 56 interventions, 44 addressed performance, 25 planning, 17 reflection, and nine the full SRL cycle. These categories overlap, so they should not be added as mutually exclusive totals. The pattern suggests that many tools show learners how they are doing, while fewer connect diagnosis to a complete plan- action- reflection sequence. The review reported a positive measurable impact in 26 studies (46%), but only nine reported improved learning outcomes (16%); only 14 studies reported enough detail for results to be interpretable and comparable. Most of the reviewed studies were in higher education (46 of 56, 82%), which further limits

direct transfer to exam- preparation settings (Heikkinen et al., 2023). The counts describe that review's included studies, not a current census of all learning analytics or a causal estimate of what a new platform will achieve.  

### 2.3 Retrieval, feedback, and spacing  

An exam- preparation system should not equate time spent viewing material with learning. Retrieval practice- attempting to recall or solve without first looking at the answer- can strengthen later retention. In two experiments, Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found that repeated testing supported better delayed retention than repeated study, although restudy could look better on an immediate test. The result is relevant to practice systems because an immediate score can reward familiarity while missing durable recall. Time- efficiency evidence makes the distinction concrete: in a comparison of 102 pharmacy students, Palmer et al. (2019) found no significant difference in one- week retention between rewatching a recorded lecture and retrieval practice, while rewatching took about three times as long. The result does not mean that rewatching is always wasteful or that the same ratio applies to exam coaching; it shows why an evaluation should measure time alongside retained learning.  

The practical implication is not "test constantly." Retrieval needs appropriate difficulty, informative feedback, and a chance to correct misconceptions. Feedback that merely reveals the right option may not explain why a distractor was tempting or what strategy to use next. Conversely, detailed feedback can consume time and overwhelm a learner if it is delivered after every trivial action. A meta- analysis of 35 articles involving 2,222 participants found positive average effects of human- machine feedback on learning processes and outcomes, with effect sizes varying across feedback direction, form, and type (Liao et al., 2024). That is evidence for feedback as a design lever, not proof that any particular feedback script or exam- preparation product is effective.  

Spacing and delayed checks add another useful constraint. If a learner answers an item correctly immediately after instruction, the evidence is compatible with short- term accessibility, not necessarily durable mastery. A later, differently worded item can test whether the learner can retrieve and apply the concept after some forgetting has occurred. In a 2025 review of applied classroom research, Mawson and Kang screened more than 3,000 records and synthesised 22 reports (31 effect estimates; more than 3,000 learners). Distributed practice outperformed massed practice on classroom learning outcomes by \(\mathrm{d} = 0.54\) (95% CI [0.31, 0.77]); heterogeneity was high ( \(\mathrm{I}^2 = 92.13\%\) ), and larger estimates tended to appear with longer retention intervals. This supports a plausible, relatively low- cost design mechanism, not a claim that any reminder schedule will produce a half- standard- deviation gain in exam preparation. A system can use delayed evidence to decide whether to advance, revisit, or mix the topic into practice. It should show the reason for that decision and permit a teacher or learner to override it.

### Enhancing knowledge tracing with concept map and response disentanglement
...
자료유형 | Article 
Content Provider | ScienceDirect 
초록 | In the rapidly advancing realm of educational technology, it becomes critical to accurately trace and understand student knowledge states. Conventional Knowledge Tracing (KT) models have mainly focused on binary responses (i.e., correct and incorrect answers) to questions. Unfortunately, they largely overlook the essential information in students’ actual answer choices, particularly for Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs), which could help reveal each learner’s misconceptions or knowledge gaps. To tackle these challenges, we propose the Concept map-driven Response disentanglement method for enhancing Knowledge Tracing (CRKT) model. CRKT benefits KT by directly leveraging answer choices – beyond merely identifying correct or incorrect answers – to distinguish responses with different incorrect choices. We further introduce the novel use of unchosen responses by employing disentangled representations to get insights from options not selected by students. Additionally, CRKT tracks the student’s knowledge state at the concept level and encodes the concept map, representing the relationships between them, to better predict unseen concepts. This approach is expected to provide actionable feedback, improving the learning experience. Our comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate CRKT’s effectiveness, achieving superior performance in prediction accuracy and interpretability over state-of-the-art models.
Highlights •Utilizing option responses for detailed insights into student knowledge states.•Introducing unchosen responses to learn the intent of the chosen response in MCQs.•Employing concept maps for enhanced interpretability and performance.•Demonstrating superior prediction performance over baselines in five datasets.•Validating effectiveness in improving personalized learning experiences.

Desirable future developments include more fine-grained assessments that provide nuanced information on students' individual biological conceptions and everyday conceptions in order to foster individualised learning (see Section 4).

### Assessment in computer science education

Students' (mis-)conceptions have also been studied for various topics in computer science education at least since the 1980s (Bayman & Mayer, 1983).

A very important topic in computer science education is traditionally programming because of its long tradition and wide-spread use. The conceptions of learners (including preconceptions and misconceptions) in this field have been investigated regarding various programming concepts. A literature review of learners' misconceptions and other difficulties is provided, for example, by Qian and Lehman (2017).

There are various (often independent) initiatives to develop concept inventories for computer science in general and for introductory programming in particular (Caceffo et al., 2016, 2019; Henry & Dumas, 2020; Rachmatullah et al., 2020).
...
(2016, 2019) use a combination of different methods (theoretical identification of fundamental concepts, analysis of students' exam solutions, and interviews) to develop a concept inventory for basic programming concepts such as parameters, variables, recursion, loops, structures, pointers and Boolean expressions. They furthermore investigate the application of the items in different programming languages and highlight the difficulty of translating misconceptions into another programming language.
...
(2020) developed a concept inventory using a block-based programming language. The items focus on similar programming concepts (variables, loops, etc.) but on a more basic level compared to Caceffo et al. (2019).

Concept inventories usually consist of single-choice or multiple choice questions. However, in the context of learning programming, a very frequent exercise format is the submission of learners' source code. Such source code is a very open answer format, but more structured/formalised compared to natural language texts.

The assessment of learners' solutions is nowadays often supported by automated assessment systems (Keuning et al., 2018), in particular due to the high and increasing number of learners in this field which makes manual assessment infeasible.
...
(2018) provide an extensive systematic literature review of automated feedback generation for programming exercises (arguably one of the most important aspects of automatic FA). They state that most automatic feedback systems mainly report errors of the submitted solutions and that only very few systems explicitly take conceptions of the learners into account.
...
(2018) furthermore find that most automatic assessment systems are not easily and flexibly adaptable by teachers to a specific learning setting. Flexible adaptions using custom models or rules are reported to be ‘too specialised and time-consuming’ (Keuning et al., 2018).

A recent literature review by Paiva et al. (2022) continues in this research direction and gives an overview of the state-of-the-art of automatic assessment in computer science education (with a focus on programming exercises). They additionally also consider aspects of LA and find that only 3 out of 30 assessment tools offer more than simple statistics for the teachers; those three tools provide in particular insights into the program development process of the learners (Paiva et al., 2022, Table 7). The authors furthermore conclude that a significant gap in this field is the lack of a standardised data format; this has partly been addressed by the proposal of Price et al.
...
For programming solutions, it is possible to infer (mis-)conceptions and competencies of learners from the submitted source code; this is often complemented by other methods like interviews or think-aloud etc. (Teague & Lister, 2014). A recent project aims to empirically identify competencies and (mis-)conceptions for object-oriented programming by performing a large-scale analysis of students' source code, complemented by manual qualitative code analyses and interviews (Krugel et al., 2020). ## Abstract

In traditional programming education, addressing diverse student needs and providing effective and scalable learning experiences is challenging. Conventional methods struggle to adapt to varying learning styles and offer personalised feedback. AI-based Programming Tools (AIPTs) have shown promise in automating feedback, simplifying programming concepts, and guiding students. Their widespread adoption is hindered by limitations related to accuracy, explanation, and personalisation. Conversely, AIPTs tailored for expert programmers, such as ChatGPT and Copilot, have gained popularity for their productivity-enhancing capabilities, but they still fall short in terms of personalisation, neglecting individual students’ unique knowledge and skills. Our research aims to leverage AI to create AIPTs that offer personalised feedback through adaptive learning, accommodating diverse student backgrounds and proficiency levels. In particular, we explore using Knowledge Tracing (KT) to anticipate specific syntax errors in programming assignments, addressing the challenges novices face in acquiring syntactical knowledge. The findings suggest the KT’s potential to transform programming education by enabling timely interventions for students dealing with specific errors or misconceptions, automating personalised feedback, and informing tailored instructional strategies.

results.summary:
While a few KT models have leveraged options in the KT scenario [8], they are still limited in obtaining robust and rich knowledge state representations.

Deep learning models have recently enhanced the capability to track complex patterns in learning data by representing knowledge states in multi-dimensional vectors [9]. While effective in capturing intricate learning trajectories, this approach often obscures the interpretability of knowledge states, making it challenging to provide actionable feedback to learners or educators [10]. In other words, representing knowledge states in multi-dimensional vector spaces does little to clarify specific areas of strength or improvement for individual learners.

Additionally, some existing models acknowledge the relevance of concepts associated with questions but largely neglect the complex relationships between these concepts [11], [12]. These concepts often serve as prerequisites for others or function within higher categories according to a learning roadmap. The inability of KT models to utilize these proper inter-concept relationships leads to a missed opportunity for achieving a comprehensive and interconnected understanding that extends beyond the concepts directly associated with individual questions.

To tackle the aforementioned limitations, we propose the Concept map-driven Response disentanglement method for enhancing Knowledge Tracing (CRKT) in this work. This innovative approach leverages detailed student responses to track knowledge states precisely. It also utilizes inter-concept relationships to access students’ latent abilities, significantly enhancing interpretability in the process.

Specifically, CRKT extends the conventional representation of correct or incorrect responses to questions into an option-based representation to utilize option responses effectively. Binary responses ignore the unique characteristics of each incorrect answer in MCQs. To illustrate this, Fig. 1(a) shows a question where the correct answer is (A), and the incorrect answers are (B), (C), and (D). Conventional KT models have treated all incorrect responses equally; however, each incorrect answer may indicate different concepts the student lacks or specific errors they have made. By leveraging option responses to differentiate among incorrect answers, CRKT not only improves the accuracy of knowledge state estimation but also enables customized interventions to meet the specific needs of learners.

In this work, we suggest utilizing both chosen and unchosen responses to obtain more precise knowledge states. Incorporating such unchosen options allows the KT model to have a more comprehensive understanding of student responses compared to utilizing only chosen option responses [7], [8]. A benefit of the proposed method is manifested in a case study in Fig. 1(a). Here, options (A), (B), and (C) correctly have the formula to compute the volume of a cylinder, while option (D) has the irrelevant formula for the volume of a sphere. If the student chooses option (D), it reflects his/her misunderstanding of geometric concepts and needs to handle them differently from other options that reflect a correct understanding of those. Overall, the proposed method is expected to reveal the reason behind the student response and distinguish each student’s strong and weak areas.

Furthermore, we enhance the interpretability of knowledge states by transitioning from conventional high-dimensional vector representations to concept-level scalar values. This shift significantly improves the utility of the KT model by making the outputs easier for educators to interpret. These interpretable knowledge states facilitate the provision of detailed, actionable feedback to learners, thereby supporting more effective personalized learning experiences.

Additionally, it is crucial to utilize the relationships among concept-level knowledge states that are obtained by integrating both chosen and unchosen responses. These relationships play a significant role in accurately predicting responses to questions involving unseen concepts. We introduce a graph-based concept map, which effectively captures relationships among concepts. The concept map used in this model is based on predefined relationships determined by experts, ensuring its relevance and effectiveness in enhancing prediction accuracy. Fig. 1(b) provides an example of how the concepts influencing the question in Fig. 1(a) are related. Assuming a student is encountering a geometry question for the first time, using the concept relations allows for accurate predictions by referencing the knowledge state of related concepts like number theory. However, if the relationships among concepts are not utilized, accurate predictions cannot be made for questions involving concepts that a student is encountering for the first time.

To effectively leverage the complex interactions between concepts, we dynamically form question-specific concept maps, considering the required conceptual understanding for each question and the relationships between related concepts. This approach ensures that the knowledge states account for the concepts directly associated with a question and their proper related concepts.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

- •We propose a novel KT model, the Concept map-driven Response disentanglement method for enhancing Knowledge Tracing (CRKT), that expands students’ binary responses to option responses and applies question-specific concept maps to trace richer knowledge states.
- •We utilize students’ unchosen responses for a more accurate understanding of students’ knowledge states. By focusing on why students selected specific options over other alternatives, we identify strengths and weaknesses that are not discernible through chosen...
